headline: 68 to 90 Feet: Sea Bass Still Jumbo, Tuna Still Working the Ridges Past the 10
subhead: The high pressure that parked over the Jersey grounds a week ago is still there, and so is the bite — from Axel Carlson Reef out to Barnegat Ridge.
body_markdown:
Sixty-eight feet. That's the number in my book next to Axel Carlson Reef this week, and it's the depth where the better sea bass have been sitting tight to structure since the middle of the month. Ninety feet does the same job out on Sea Girt Reef. Neither number has moved much in ten days, which tells you almost everything about why the fishing has stayed consistent — the water hasn't been pushed around, the bottom temp hasn't crashed, and the bait hasn't scattered.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the warm filament sitting on the ridges and reef edges would hold the bite together as long as high pressure stayed put, and that's exactly what's happened. No fronts, no dirty water, no big wind events to blow the structure out. That kind of stability is rare for late August in this stretch of the Bight, and it's the reason the tuna work out on Klondike and Barnegat Ridge has kept producing instead of going quiet the way it usually does once the calendar flips toward Labor Day.

The sea bass grounds have been the most dependable part of the week. Axel Carlson Reef and Sea Girt Reef are both holding fish in the 60 to 90-foot range, and the better ones — 3 and 4 pounds, some pushing bigger — are coming off the high-relief pieces rather than the open sand between wrecks. Standard high-low rigs baited with clam and squid strips are doing the work; there's no need to get fancy right now, the fish are eating the bottom bait as fast as it goes down. Shrewsbury Rocks has been a touch spottier — good pockets of keeper-class fish mixed with a lot of short teasers, so it pays to move around rather than anchor on the first mark that shows fish on the sounder. Triple Wrecks has been the sleeper this week, producing some of the better mixed bags — sea bass stacked with the occasional ling — for boats willing to make the extra run and work the pieces methodically instead of drifting through once and leaving.

Offshore, the tuna picture has stayed better than it usually is this deep into summer. Yellowfin and some bluefin have been working the temperature breaks out past Klondike and along Barnegat Ridge, and the mix of species reported out there — with mahi mixed in around the color changes and current lines — is unusual for this time of year in water this close to the beach. Trolling small spreads of cedar plugs and green machines has been the more consistent producer over straight bird-and-ballyhoo rigs, and boats willing to chunk once they mark fish have had better luck closing the deal than the ones running-and-gunning all day. Mahi have been scattered around whatever current edges and floating structure hold bait — nothing stacked up in big numbers, but enough for a mixed cooler if you're willing to put in the running time and check a few lines rather than sit on one spot.

The moon is building toward full over the next several nights, and that's going to matter more than people think. Bigger tidal swings mean more water moving across the reef structure, which usually tightens up bait concentrations rather than spreading them out — that's typically good news for the reef bite, less predictable for the open-water tuna work where bait can get pushed off the temperature lines. Expect the sea bass bite to hold or even improve slightly as the tide flow increases over the reefs; expect the offshore bite to stay a little more day-to-day as boats chase whichever line holds the warm water best.

With Labor Day weekend on the horizon, boat traffic is going to pick up fast across all of these grounds, and that's worth planning around. The reef structure — Axel Carlson, Sea Girt, Shrewsbury Rocks — gets crowded on a holiday weekend, and anchoring rights on the better pieces go to whoever gets there first. If you're set on fishing one of the wreck numbers rather than the open reef, get out early; the good pieces on Triple Wrecks only hold so many boats before the bite gets picked over.

Looking at the next 72 hours, the pattern should hold if the high pressure stays where it is. That's the wildcard worth watching — nothing organized in the tropics yet that threatens this stretch, but late August into early September is exactly the window when that can change fast. If the weather stays quiet, Barnegat Ridge and Klondike should keep producing tuna and mahi on the troll, and the reef network should keep giving up jumbo sea bass on bottom rigs through the holiday weekend. If a system starts spinning up in the western Atlantic, that's the signal to shift plans inside and work the closer wrecks rather than committing to a long run offshore. For now, the numbers in the book are holding steady, and that's about as good a sign as this time of year offers.
